title: Levodopa-Responsive Primary Slow Orthostatic Tremor: A Premotor Sign of Parkinson's Disease?
case_prompt:
A 63-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of leg tremor and unsteadiness on standing. Her medical history was notable only for remote angina; she was not taking psychotropic medications. On standing, she had incessant quivering of the lower limbs that disappeared on walking, sitting, or leaning against support. Fine rippling of the quadriceps muscles was observed, with no tremor elsewhere. Examination showed no bradykinesia, rigidity, gait disturbance, supranuclear gaze palsy, cerebellar signs, autonomic dysfunction, restless legs syndrome, cognitive impairment, REM sleep behavior disorder, or insomnia. Alcohol did not alleviate the tremor, and there was no family history of tremor or parkinsonism.  
   
Laboratory studies (CBC, electrolytes, glucose, renal and liver function, vitamin B12, thyroid function), chest radiography, and EEG were normal. Brain MRI revealed only small cerebral white-matter infarctions. Surface EMG of the lower legs demonstrated rhythmic motor unit potentials at 5–6 Hz, with burst durations of 100 ms and amplitudes of 200–400 µV; bursts were larger on the right than the left and were not coherent across muscles. No discharges occurred when supine or sitting with the feet dangling.  
   
A [123I]-FP-CIT DAT-SPECT study showed specific binding ratios of 3.31 in the right striatum and 3.50 in the left striatum, values decreased compared with age-matched controls.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Typical orthostatic tremor is unlikely given the low tremor frequency — “OT is defined as a rapid tremor ... with a characteristic frequency of 13–18 Hz … tremor frequency of our patient was 5–6 Hz, which is consistent with slow OT.”  
2. Secondary orthostatic tremor was excluded because there were no additional neurological features — “Because our patient did not show any other neurological disorders, we diagnosed her tremor as primary OT.”  
3. Orthostatic myoclonus was excluded on the basis of EMG and clinical features — “clinical features and EMG findings exclude OM in our case.”  
4. Parkinson’s disease was considered due to similar tremor frequency and reduced DAT binding but was deemed unlikely in the absence of bradykinesia, rigidity, or gait disturbance — “No parkinsonian signs such as bradykinesia, muscle rigidity, or gait disturbance ... were found.”
